disclaimer: This is an automated screening aid, not a confirmed diagnosis. Confirm with a local agriculture extension officer or plant pathologist before treating. Always follow product labels and local regulations when using any chemical.

healthy.name: Healthy
symptoms: No visible signs of disease were detected on this leaf.
prevention: Water at the base of plants and avoid wetting leaves late in the day.
Space plants for good airflow and remove plant debris regularly.
Rotate crops and use certified, disease-free seed or seedlings.
management: No treatment is needed.
Keep scouting weekly, especially after rain or humid spells, and re-check if spots, curling or discoloration appear.

apple_scab.name: Apple scab
symptoms: Olive-green to brown, velvety spots on leaves that darken and may twist the leaf.
Scabby, corky patches on fruit; badly infected leaves yellow and drop early.
prevention: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to remove the fungus's winter home.
Prune for open canopy so leaves dry quickly.
Plant scab-resistant varieties where possible.
management: Apply a protectant fungicide labelled for apples from bud break, following your local spray guide.
Remove heavily infected leaves and fruit.
Avoid overhead irrigation.

apple_black_rot.name: Apple black rot
symptoms: 'Frogeye' leaf spots: purple-edged spots with a tan centre.
Fruit rots with dark concentric rings and may shrivel into hard black mummies; cankers can form on branches.
prevention: Prune out dead wood and cankers during dormancy.
Remove mummified fruit from trees and the ground.
Protect trees from wounds and insect damage.
management: Cut out cankers back to healthy wood and remove the debris from the orchard.
Use a fungicide programme labelled for apples as advised locally.
Pick off and destroy infected fruit.

cedar_apple_rust.name: Cedar apple rust
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface, often with tiny tube-like projections underneath.
Similar lesions can appear on fruit; heavy infection causes early leaf drop.
prevention: Remove nearby juniper or red cedar trees where practical, as they host the fungus.
Choose rust-resistant apple varieties.
management: Apply a protectant fungicide labelled for apples from pink bud through early summer, as advised locally.
Prune out galls on nearby junipers in late winter.

cherry_powdery_mildew.name: Powdery mildew (cherry)
symptoms: White, powdery fungal growth on leaves and shoot tips.
Leaves may curl, distort or turn purplish and drop early.
prevention: Prune for airflow and sunlight.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertiliser, which promotes soft growth.
Water in the morning at the soil level.
management: Prune out and destroy infected shoots.
Apply sulfur or another fungicide labelled for cherries at first sign, as advised locally.

corn_gray_leaf_spot.name: Gray leaf spot (corn)
symptoms: Narrow, rectangular tan to gray lesions running parallel to the leaf veins.
Lesions merge in humid weather and can blight whole leaves.
prevention: Rotate away from corn for at least a year.
Bury or break down crop residue after harvest.
Plant tolerant hybrids.
management: Scout fields and consider a labelled fungicide if lesions reach the upper leaves before or around tasseling in humid weather.
Avoid planting corn after corn in the same field.

corn_common_rust.name: Common rust (corn)
symptoms: Small, round to elongated, reddish-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces.
Pustules release powdery rust-coloured spores that rub off on fingers.
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids.
Plant at the recommended time so young plants avoid cool, humid spells.
management: Often minor; monitor spread to the upper leaves.
Consider a labelled fungicide only if infection is heavy before tasseling.

corn_northern_leaf_blight.name: Northern leaf blight (corn)
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped gray-green to tan lesions, several centimetres long, on the leaves.
Lesions can join together and blight large areas of the leaf.
prevention: Use resistant hybrids.
Rotate crops and manage residue by tillage or decomposition.
management: Scout from early growth and consider a labelled fungicide if lesions appear on upper leaves around tasseling.
Remove or bury infected residue after harvest.

grape_black_rot.name: Grape black rot
symptoms: Tan spots with dark borders on leaves, with tiny black dots inside.
Berries brown, shrivel and turn into hard black mummies.
prevention: Remove mummified berries and infected canes during dormancy.
Keep the canopy open so leaves and fruit dry quickly.
management: Apply a protectant fungicide from early shoot growth through fruit set, as advised locally.
Remove and destroy infected clusters.

grape_esca.name: Grape esca (black measles)
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' yellow or brown patches between the leaf veins.
Dark spots on berries; cut wood shows dark streaks, and vines can collapse suddenly.
prevention: Prune in dry weather and protect large pruning cuts with a wound sealant.
Use clean, certified planting stock.
management: There is no cure; remove and destroy dead or severely affected wood and vines.
Do not leave prunings in the vineyard, and ask your extension service about local options.

grape_leaf_blight.name: Grape leaf blight (Isariopsis leaf spot)
symptoms: Irregular dark brown spots on leaves, usually on older leaves first.
Severely affected leaves yellow and drop early.
prevention: Keep the canopy open and remove fallen leaves.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
management: Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Use a fungicide programme labelled for grapes, as advised locally.

citrus_greening.name: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling of leaves, and yellow shoots.
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the bottom and drops early.
prevention: Control the Asian citrus psyllid that spreads the disease.
Plant only certified disease-free nursery trees.
management: There is no cure. Report suspected cases to your local agriculture authority.
Infected trees are usually removed to protect others; follow local regulations.

bacterial_spot.name: Bacterial spot
symptoms: Small, water-soaked dark spots on leaves that turn brown or black, sometimes with a yellow halo.
Rough, scabby spots on fruit; heavily affected leaves yellow and drop.
prevention: Use certified clean seed or transplants.
Avoid overhead irrigation and do not work among wet plants.
Rotate away from the crop for 2 to 3 years.
management: Remove and destroy infected plants or leaves.
Copper-based bactericides can slow spread but will not cure existing spots.
Disinfect tools between plants.

early_blight.name: Early blight
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings like a target, usually starting on older lower leaves.
Yellowing around the spots; stems and fruit can also show lesions.
prevention: Rotate crops and remove plant debris at the end of the season.
Mulch and use drip irrigation to stop soil splashing onto leaves.
Give plants enough nutrients and space.
management: Remove infected lower leaves.
Apply a fungicide labelled for the crop at first symptoms, as advised locally.

late_blight.name: Late blight
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked blotches on leaves that turn brown or black.
White fuzzy growth on leaf undersides in humid weather; fruit and tubers can rot. It spreads very fast.
prevention: Use certified seed and destroy volunteer plants and cull piles.
Avoid overhead watering and improve airflow.
Plant resistant varieties where available.
management: Act quickly: remove and bag infected plants; do not compost them.
Apply a protectant fungicide labelled for the crop as advised locally, and alert neighbouring growers.
Do not store tubers or fruit from affected plants.

squash_powdery_mildew.name: Powdery mildew (squash)
symptoms: White, powdery patches on the upper leaf surface and stems.
Leaves yellow, dry out and die, reducing yield.
prevention: Plant in full sun with wide spacing.
Choose resistant varieties.
Avoid excess nitrogen.
management: Remove badly infected leaves.
Apply sulfur, potassium bicarbonate or a fungicide labelled for squash at first sign.

strawberry_leaf_scorch.name: Strawberry leaf scorch
symptoms: Many small purple spots on leaves that enlarge and merge.
Leaves look scorched, dry and may curl.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties and space plants for airflow.
Renovate beds and remove old leaves after harvest.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
management: Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Apply a fungicide labelled for strawberries if disease is spreading, as advised locally.

leaf_mold.name: Tomato leaf mold
symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots on the upper leaf surface.
Olive-green to brown velvety mold on the underside, mainly in humid, enclosed conditions.
prevention: Ventilate greenhouses and lower humidity.
Space and stake plants; choose resistant varieties.
management: Prune lower infected leaves and keep foliage dry.
Use a fungicide labelled for tomatoes if it keeps spreading.

septoria_leaf_spot.name: Septoria leaf spot
symptoms: Many small circular spots with gray-white centres and dark borders.
Tiny black specks in the centres; starts on lower leaves, which then yellow and drop.
prevention: Rotate crops and clear plant debris.
Mulch and water at the base of plants.
management: Remove infected lower leaves.
Apply a fungicide labelled for the crop at first signs, as advised locally.

spider_mites.name: Spider mite damage
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on leaves, which may turn bronze.
Fine webbing on leaf undersides; leaves dry out and drop, worst in hot, dry weather.
prevention: Avoid water stress and dusty conditions.
Encourage natural predators and scout undersides of leaves regularly.
management: Wash mites off with a strong spray of water.
Use insecticidal soap, horticultural oil or a miticide labelled for the crop; avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators.

target_spot.name: Target spot
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings on leaves, sometimes on stems and fruit.
Looks similar to early blight.
prevention: Improve airflow, rotate crops and remove crop debris.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
management: Remove infected leaves.
Apply a fungicide labelled for the crop as advised locally.

tylcv.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
symptoms: Leaves curl upward and cup, with yellow edges.
Plants are stunted and bushy, with flower drop and poor fruit set.
prevention: Control whiteflies using screens, reflective mulch and monitoring.
Plant resistant varieties and certified virus-free transplants.
management: There is no cure; remove and destroy infected plants early.
Control whiteflies and remove nearby weeds that host the virus.

tomato_mosaic_virus.name: Tomato mosaic virus
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves.
Distorted, fern-like leaves, stunted plants and uneven fruit ripening.
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed.
Wash hands and disinfect tools; avoid handling tobacco before touching plants.
Remove weeds that can host the virus.
management: There is no cure; remove and destroy infected plants, and do not compost them.
Disinfect tools and supports before reuse.

soybean_bacterial_blight.name: Soybean bacterial blight
symptoms: Small angular, water-soaked spots that turn brown with a yellow halo.
Spots merge and centres can tear out, leaving ragged leaves.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and resistant varieties.
Rotate away from soybean and bury crop residue.
Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet.
management: There is no cure; copper sprays give only limited help.
Avoid moving through wet fields to stop spreading it.
Rotate crops next season.

soybean_cercospora_leaf_blight.name: Soybean Cercospora leaf blight
symptoms: Upper leaves turn leathery and purple to bronze, often with small light purple spots.
Severe cases cause leaf drop; seeds can show purple staining.
prevention: Rotate crops and manage residue.
Use clean seed and avoid dense planting.
management: Scout from flowering; if widespread, consider a labelled foliar fungicide around pod set as advised locally.
Remove or bury infected residue after harvest.

soybean_downy_mildew.name: Soybean downy mildew
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface.
Grayish fuzzy growth on the underside; spots turn brown.
prevention: Use resistant varieties and clean seed.
Rotate crops and manage residue.
management: Usually causes limited yield loss; monitor spread.
A fungicide is rarely needed; ask your extension service if infection is heavy.

soybean_frogeye_leaf_spot.name: Soybean frogeye leaf spot
symptoms: Circular to angular spots with gray-tan centres and dark reddish-brown borders.
Heavily spotted leaves can die and drop.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Rotate crops and bury residue.
Use clean seed.
management: If widespread around flowering and pod fill, apply a labelled foliar fungicide as advised locally.
Avoid soybean after soybean in the same field.

soybean_rust.name: Soybean rust
symptoms: Tiny tan to reddish-brown pustules, mostly on the underside of leaves.
Leaves yellow and drop early; spreads quickly by wind.
prevention: Scout regularly, especially in warm humid weather.
Plant earlier-maturing varieties where suitable.
Remove volunteer soybean and alternate host plants.
management: Act quickly: apply a labelled foliar fungicide when rust is found, following local advisories.
Report outbreaks to your agriculture extension service.

soybean_target_spot.name: Soybean target spot
symptoms: Brown circular spots with concentric rings and a yellow halo.
Often starts on the lower canopy and moves upward.
prevention: Rotate crops and bury residue.
Avoid overly dense canopies so leaves dry quickly.
management: Apply a labelled fungicide if disease is severe in humid weather, as advised locally.
Remove or bury infected residue.

soybean_potassium_deficiency.name: Soybean potassium deficiency
symptoms: Yellowing then browning along leaf edges and tips, starting on older leaves.
Plants may look stunted with poor pod fill.
prevention: Test soil before planting and keep potassium at recommended levels.
Avoid soil compaction and drought stress.
management: Apply potassium fertiliser based on a soil or leaf test.
Correct soil pH if it is out of range; do not spray fungicide for this problem.

wheat_yellow_rust.name: Wheat yellow (stripe) rust
symptoms: Stripes of yellow-orange pustules running along the leaf veins.
Leaves dry out early; worst in cool, humid weather.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Remove volunteer wheat that carries rust between seasons.
Avoid very early sowing.
management: Scout often; if rust reaches the upper leaves, apply a labelled fungicide quickly as advised locally.
Report outbreaks to your agriculture extension service.

wheat_brown_rust.name: Wheat brown (leaf) rust
symptoms: Scattered round orange-brown pustules mainly on the upper leaf surface.
Leaves yellow and dry; yield drops if the flag leaf is hit.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Remove volunteer wheat and sow at the recommended time.
management: If pustules are on the flag leaf before grain filling, apply a labelled fungicide as advised locally.
Keep scouting every few days in warm, humid weather.

wheat_septoria.name: Septoria leaf blotch (wheat)
symptoms: Yellow to brown blotches limited by the leaf veins, starting on lower leaves.
Tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) appear inside the lesions in wet weather.
prevention: Rotate crops and manage stubble.
Use resistant varieties and avoid very dense sowing.
management: Protect the upper leaves with a labelled fungicide timed to the flag-leaf stage, as advised locally.
Remove or bury infected residue after harvest.

wheat_powdery_mildew.name: Wheat powdery mildew
symptoms: White fluffy powdery colonies on leaves and stems.
Colonies turn gray-brown with black specks as they age.
prevention: Use resistant varieties.
Avoid excess nitrogen and overly dense stands.
management: Apply a labelled fungicide if it is spreading to upper leaves, as advised locally.
Manage stubble and volunteer wheat.

rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.name: Rice bacterial leaf blight
symptoms: Water-soaked yellow-orange stripes along leaf edges that turn straw-coloured and dry.
Seedlings can wilt and die ('kresek').
prevention: Use certified seed and resistant varieties.
Avoid excess nitrogen and keep fields well drained.
Remove infected stubble and weeds.
management: There is no cure; reduce nitrogen and drain the field.
Copper products give only limited help.
Avoid moving water or tools from infected to healthy fields.

rice_brown_spot.name: Rice brown spot
symptoms: Oval brown spots with gray centres and yellow halos on leaves.
Can spread to grains, causing discoloured, lighter kernels.
prevention: Use healthy, treated seed.
Fertilise in balance and fix nutrient shortages.
Avoid water stress.
management: Improve soil fertility and water management.
Apply a labelled fungicide if infection is severe, as advised locally.

rice_leaf_blast.name: Rice leaf blast
symptoms: Diamond or spindle-shaped lesions with gray centres and brown borders.
Can kill seedlings and later cause neck blast (broken panicle necks).
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and use treated seed.
Avoid heavy single doses of nitrogen.
Avoid late planting.
management: Apply a labelled fungicide at early symptoms, as advised locally.
Manage field water and split nitrogen applications.

rice_tungro.name: Rice tungro disease
symptoms: Yellow to orange discolouration of leaves.
Stunted plants with fewer tillers and poor grain.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and synchronise planting in the area.
Control leafhoppers and remove infected stubble and weeds.
management: There is no cure; remove infected plants early where practical.
Control leafhopper vectors and avoid planting next to infected fields.

rice_leaf_smut.name: Rice leaf smut
symptoms: Small, angular, raised black spots or smudges on both sides of the leaf.
prevention: Use healthy seed and balanced fertiliser.
Remove infected crop residue.
management: Usually a minor disease; monitor.
A fungicide is rarely needed; ask your extension service if it is severe.

rice_leaf_scald.name: Rice leaf scald
symptoms: Lesions start at leaf tips and edges, with bands that give a scalded look.
Leaves dry from the tip downward.
prevention: Use clean seed and resistant varieties.
Avoid excess nitrogen.
management: Remove heavily infected residue.
Apply a labelled fungicide if severe, as advised locally.

rice_sheath_blight.name: Rice sheath blight
symptoms: Oval greenish-gray lesions on leaf sheaths near the water line.
Lesions turn grayish-white with brown borders and spread upward.
prevention: Avoid dense planting and heavy nitrogen.
Control weeds and remove infected straw and stubble.
management: Apply a labelled fungicide from tillering to booting if disease is spreading, as advised locally.
Drain the field where possible.

cotton_bacterial_blight.name: Cotton bacterial blight
symptoms: Angular water-soaked spots limited by leaf veins that turn brown.
Dark lesions can form on stems ('black arm') and bolls.
prevention: Use certified, delinted seed and resistant varieties.
Rotate crops and destroy infected residue.
management: There is no cure; copper sprays may slow spread.
Avoid working in wet fields and remove badly infected plants.

cotton_curl_virus.name: Cotton leaf curl virus
symptoms: Leaves curl upward or downward with thickened, dark veins.
Plants are stunted; small leaf-like growths can appear under the leaf.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and sow on time.
Control whiteflies and remove weed hosts.
management: There is no cure; uproot early-infected plants.
Manage whiteflies with integrated methods as advised locally.

cotton_fusarium_wilt.name: Cotton Fusarium wilt
symptoms: Yellowing and wilting of lower leaves, often on one side of the plant.
Cut stems show brown streaks inside.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Rotate crops and control root-knot nematodes.
Avoid injuring roots.
management: There is no cure; remove and destroy infected plants.
Do not move soil or water from infected fields to clean ones.

cotton_verticillium_wilt.name: Cotton Verticillium wilt
symptoms: Yellow patches between the veins that turn brown, plus wilting.
Cut stems show brown discolouration inside.
prevention: Rotate with non-host crops such as cereals.
Use tolerant varieties and keep fields clean of residue.
management: There is no cure; remove infected residue.
Avoid excess nitrogen and over-irrigation.

cotton_alternaria_leaf_spot.name: Cotton Alternaria leaf spot
symptoms: Small brown spots with concentric rings and purple margins.
Spots merge and leaves may drop early.
prevention: Rotate crops and remove residue.
Keep potassium and nutrition balanced.
management: Remove infected residue after harvest.
Apply a labelled fungicide if severe, as advised locally.

sugarcane_red_rot.name: Sugarcane red rot
symptoms: Red discolouration inside split stalks with white cross bands.
Reddish spots on the leaf midrib and drying of the top leaves.
prevention: Plant disease-free setts from healthy fields; consider heat treatment of setts.
Use resistant varieties and rotate crops.
management: Uproot and destroy infected clumps; do not use setts from infected fields.
Avoid ratooning a heavily infected crop; ask your extension service about local control.

sugarcane_rust.name: Sugarcane rust
symptoms: Small, elongated orange-brown pustules on both sides of the leaf.
Heavily infected leaves dry out early.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties.
Avoid excess nitrogen.
management: Remove heavily infected leaves.
Apply a labelled fungicide if severe, as advised locally.

sugarcane_mosaic.name: Sugarcane mosaic
sugarcane_mosaic.cause: viral (spread by aphids and infected setts)
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green streaks along the leaf.
Stunted growth and thinner stalks.
prevention: Use virus-free seed cane and resistant varieties.
Control aphids.
management: There is no cure; remove infected plants early.
Do not take setts from infected fields.

sugarcane_yellow_leaf.name: Sugarcane yellow leaf disease
sugarcane_yellow_leaf.cause: viral (spread by aphids and infected setts)
symptoms: Yellowing of the leaf midrib on the underside, spreading across the blade.
Leaves dry from the tips; growth is reduced.
prevention: Use virus-free seed cane (for example tissue-culture plantlets) and resistant varieties.
Control aphids.
management: There is no cure; remove infected stools where practical.
Avoid ratooning heavily infected crops.
